1. Outcome — Largely for Taylor. The Court of Chancery (Laster, V.C.) granted summary judgment compelling Calm to advance Taylor’s defense costs (with interest and fees-on-fees), denying Calm’s contrary declaratory claims. Advancement was denied only for any counts based solely on post‑employment restrictive-covenant breaches.

2. Reasoning — Applying DGCL §145 and Calm’s mandatory advancement provisions, the court held the underlying claims against Taylor arose “by reason of the fact” of his corporate service (e.g., decisions and conduct in office and use of information obtained as an officer), so advancement was required; Calm’s arguments about alleged bad acts or ultimate liability go to indemnification, not advancement. To the extent certain claims rested purely on post‑termination contractual obligations independent of corporate capacity, they were not covered. Calm’s attempts to condition or delay payment were rejected, and Taylor received fees-on-fees for enforcing his right.
